questions.q: What is the real, correct order of a contract's life cycle, per this lesson?
questions.explain: You write the Solidity code first, compile it into bytecode, deploy it to the blockchain, and only then can anyone interact with it.

questions.q: What real error did the instructor demonstrate live when the pragma and the selected compiler version didn't match?
options: No error occurs when they don't match
questions.explain: Remix flagged a real compiler error — the source file's pragma (0.8.30) didn't match the compiler version selected (0.8.27) — until the instructor changed the compiler to match.

questions.q: What does compiling a Solidity contract actually output?
options: Bytecode — the low-level format the EVM can execute
questions.explain: Compiling converts human-readable Solidity into bytecode, the format the EVM actually understands and executes.

questions.q: In the instructor's own words, what did he say about the raw bytecode after compiling?
options: "This doesn't make any sense to me, but the EVM understands this and it represents what the code is"
"This is exactly as readable as the original Solidity"
"Bytecode is optional and can be skipped"
questions.explain: The instructor was direct about it: the bytecode is unreadable to humans, but it's exactly what the EVM needs to actually run the contract.

questions.q: In the finished contract from this lesson, what real structure does each variable (message, alphabet, color) follow?
options: A data type, a name, and a value — a key-value pair
Just a name with no value
A function with no data type
A pragma statement for each variable
questions.explain: Each line follows the same pattern: a string data type, a name (like message), and a quoted value — the same key-value structure used later in JSON and the ABI.
